name: Stillman's Freckle Cream

lead: Stillman's Freckle Cream was a patent-medicine freckle remover made by a company in Aurora, Illinois, and sold in the early 20th century. It was used to fade freckles and lighten the complexion toward an even, pale tone.

Freckle removers of its type, including Stillman's, commonly contained mercury compounds such as ammoniated mercury and bichloride of mercury. Mercury skin products are now restricted or banned in many countries.

paras: Historically users applied a thin layer of the cream to freckled areas, typically at night, and continued for weeks. Products were sold in several strengths.

Mercury compounds absorb through the skin and can cause skin discoloration, peeling, nerve symptoms, memory problems and kidney damage. The US moved in the 1940s to cap ammoniated mercury at 5% with warnings, and mercury cosmetics were restricted or banned in the US, UK and EU by the 1970s.

chain: Mercury compounds interfere with surface pigment and exfoliate skin
angle.text: Users applied it to fade freckles and lighten tone. Its actions came from mercury compounds, whose toxicity is the reason the category is now restricted.

lead: Stillman's Freckle Cream was a freckle remover sold by the Stillman Freckle Cream Co. of Aurora, Illinois, as shown in a 1906 drugstore advertisement [1]. It was marketed to people who wanted freckles faded and a lighter, more even complexion.

Reference writing on historical beauty products names Stillman's among the commonly used freckle removers that contained mercury compounds, alongside Othine and Berry's Freckle Ointment [2]. These were typically ammoniated mercury or bichloride of mercury, sometimes combined with bismuth or zinc salts, and some double and triple strength versions reached 10 to 15 percent or more [2].
infobox: Stillman Freckle Cream Co., Aurora, Illinois (1906 ad) [1]

paras: Freckle removers were a staple of Victorian and Edwardian beauty literature [2]. A 1906 Milwaukee Drug Company advertisement lists the Stillman Freckle Cream Co. of Aurora, Illinois as manufacturer [1]. A reference page on freckle removers shows Stillman's packaging from 1929 and 1956 [2]. A 1948 trademark record lists The Stillman Company, Inc. in Aurora [3].

Commercial freckle creams used ammoniated mercury and bichloride of mercury, often with bismuth or zinc salts [2]. After the 1938 Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, the US FDA in the 1940s moved to limit mercury compounds to 5% or less, and some products were seized and destroyed [2]. Mercury-containing cosmetics remained on the market until the 1970s, when the UK, US, EU and others restricted or banned them [2].

Mercury(II) chloride absorbs readily through skin. Symptoms of mercury poisoning from skin-whitening products include tingling or burning, skin discoloration and peeling, muscle weakness, memory problems, anxiety, insomnia and kidney problems [4].

In 2010 a Chicago Tribune investigation reported a Pakistani-made whitener sold under the Stillman name that contained nearly 30,000 ppm mercury; the owner said the Pakistani company had been authorised in the 1970s to sell skin whiteners under the name only in Pakistan [5].
